executive_summary: The defining thread running through today's content is the tension between institutional legitimacy and reactionary backlash — who holds power, who is being displaced, and how those facing disruption respond. The Atlantic's deep investigation into masculinism as the ideological core of the American right makes explicit what The Economist's note on Trump's continued political revenge-seeking illustrates in practice: a movement that frames legitimate social progress as existential loss and channels that grievance into systematic rollback of hard-won rights. The Atlantic is unambiguous that masculinism's central claim — that feminism has ruined America — is empirically unsupported, yet its political potency is real, as evidenced by its fusion with mainstream conservative governance. Meanwhile, MIT Technology Review's report on Colossal Biosciences engineering life inside 3D-printed artificial eggshells serves as an unexpected counterpoint: it represents the opposite impulse — not reversal of progress, but an almost audacious acceleration of it, reengineering biological systems rather than retreating from complexity. Taken together, today's content maps a society simultaneously racing toward futures it hasn't fully reckoned with and fighting pitched battles to reclaim a past that never existed as advertised.

newsletters.title: Colossal Biosciences is growing chickens in a 3D-printed artificial eggshell

items.headline: Colossal Biosciences is growing chickens in a 3D-printed artificial eggshell
items.blurb:
The baby chicks were shifting and starting to pip—or trying to hatch. But not from an egg. Instead, these chickens were growing inside transparent 3D-printed plastic cups at the Dallas headquarters of Colossal Biosciences.

The biotech company yesterday claimed it has developed a "fully artificial egg" as part of its effort to resurrect extinct avian species, including birds like the dodo and the giant moa.

Some scientists think Colossal is overstating the breakthrough. But the technology may represent an early step toward artificial wombs.

items.headline: Inside the Musk v. Altman Trial
items.blurb:
Elon Musk has lost his landmark lawsuit against OpenAI, which centered on allegations that its cofounders Sam Altman and Greg Brockman misled him about the company's nonprofit mission. But what really happened in the courtroom, and what does it mean for the AI race?

AI reporter and attorney Michelle Kim, who covered the trial for MIT Technology Review, joined our editor in chief Mat Honan to unpack it all in an exclusive Roundtables discussion yesterday.

items.headline: MIT Technology Review Narrated: this scientist rewarmed and studied pieces of his friend's cryopreserved brain
items.blurb:
L. Stephen Coles's brain sits in a vat at a storage facility in Arizona. It has been held there at a temperature of around −146 degrees °C for over a decade, largely undisturbed. Before he died in 2014, Coles had the brain frozen with an ambitious goal in mind: reanimation.

His friend, cryobiologist Greg Fahy, believes it could be revived one day. But other experts are less optimistic.

Still, Fahy's research could lead to new ways to study the brain. And using cryopreservation for organ transplantation is becoming a viable reality.

items.headline: Can AI learn to understand the world?
items.blurb:
The limitations of LLMs are pushing AI researchers towards new systems that understand the physical environment: world models. The likes of Google DeepMind, Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, and Meta's former Chief AI Scientist, AI Yann LeCun, have brought this technology to the forefront of AI.

To explore where this technology is heading next, MIT Technology Review is hosting an exclusive Roundtables discussion on Thursday, May 21, with editor in chief Mat Honan, senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven, and AI reporter Grace Huckins.

items.headline: Who's writing this?
items.blurb: "The Future of Truth" is the title of a new book about what artificial intelligence is doing to veracity. Steven Rosenbaum, its author, used artificial intelligence to help him research, write and edit. The Times took a close look at the book and found more than a half-dozen misattributed or completely made-up quotes concocted by A.I., including one stemwinder from the tech journalist Kara Swisher. It wasn't just wrong, Swisher said, but "I also sound like I have a stick up my butt." Rosenbaum acknowledged the delusions, telling our reporter that if the hallucination "serves as a warning about the risks of A.I.-assisted research and verification, that is why I wrote the book."

items.headline: Google to overhaul search bar for A.I.
items.blurb: Yesterday, Google announced that it will overhaul the search bar it has used for the past 25 years to accommodate longer, more complex questions answered by A.I.

items.headline: University of Arizona graduates boo Eric Schmidt at commencement
items.blurb: Graduating students at the University of Arizona last week booed their commencement speaker, the former Google leader Eric Schmidt. He had been talking about the vast promise of A.I. to transform the world through technology. Graduates didn't want to hear it.

items.headline: Job security
items.blurb: China's courts are trying to balance widespread A.I. adoption with the unemployment it may bring about. One precedent-setting decision recently said that an employee couldn't be fired after he'd been replaced by software. China is an A.I. leader, but it also has a high youth unemployment rate — about 17 percent. Some 200 million people work gig-economy jobs. Officials in Japan, South Korea and Britain have proposed versions of a universal basic income for workers displaced by technology.

newsletters.title: A wild comeback in New York

items.headline: The Knicks' comeback
items.blurb: With 7:40 left in the fourth quarter, the visiting Cavaliers led the Knicks 93-71. Vibes were bad. A big Game 1 atmosphere went poof. Jalen Brunson then got to work. He scored 15 in the fourth quarter amid a 30-8 New York run. Regulation ended in a 101-101 tie, and the Knicks reeled off a 14-3 overtime advantage. Just like that: New York is three wins away from the finals.

items.headline: Arsenal's crowning
items.blurb: Arsenal has officially won the 2026 Premier League title after Manchester City drew against AFC Bournemouth yesterday. It is a title 22 years in the making, and crystallizes how good the club has been all season. It was an emotional day for everyone involved.

items.headline: Southampton banished from Championship play-off final
items.blurb: The English Football League officially banished Southampton from the Championship play-off final — which will determine a Premier League spot next year — after the club admitted to spying on rival teams. Missing out on an EPL slot means no shot at an extra £200 million (about $270M) in broadcast revenue that Premier League teams earn. Southampton players are considering legal action against the club.

items.headline: Rice gets jail time
items.blurb: Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice is spending 30 days in jail for violating his probation, according to Dallas court logs, and will likely miss OTAs. The probation stems from his involvement in a high-profile car crash in Dallas two years ago. Rice, 26, is set for release on June 16, five days after OTAs end.

items.headline: Kidd, Mavs part ways
items.blurb: Jason Kidd is out as coach of the Mavericks, ending a fascinating five-year tenure as lead man of a franchise for which he played. Kidd, along with star Luka Dončić, led Dallas to the finals in 2023-24. In the years following, the franchise sold to new owners, traded Dončić, drafted Cooper Flagg and hired Masai Ujiri as president of basketball operations.

items.headline: Alcaraz to miss Wimbledon
items.blurb: Tennis superstar Carlos Alcaraz will miss a second straight major this season at Wimbledon, where he's won twice, because of a wrist injury. He lost the championship match last year to Jannik Sinner, of course, who figures to be the overwhelming favorite next month. The last time a man not named Sinner or Alcaraz won a Grand Slam: Novak Djokovic in 2023.

items.headline: A little-league grand slam
items.blurb: James Wood hit an inside-the-park grand slam for the Nationals against the Mets.

newsletters.title: The US in Brief: Trump gets more revenge

items.headline: Thomas Massie defeated in primary
items.blurb: Thomas Massie became the latest casualty of Donald Trump's purge of Republican dissenters. Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL backed by the president, defeated the Kentucky congressman in a primary. Mr Trump campaigned aggressively against Mr Massie, who has criticised the president's handling of Iran and the Epstein files. Bill Cassidy, a senator from Louisiana, and several Indiana lawmakers who crossed Mr Trump have also lost primary battles recently.

items.headline: Trump's allies do well in Georgia primaries
items.blurb: Mike Collins, a congressman, finished first in a primary to represent the Republican Party in a Senate race. He now enters a run-off. Burt Jones, whom Mr Trump endorsed, came first in the race to be the Republican nominee for governor, and will face Rick Jackson, a healthcare executive, in a run-off. Brad Raffensperger, who resisted Mr Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election, finished a distant third.

items.headline: Trump endorses Ken Paxton in Texas Senate race
items.blurb: The president endorsed Ken Paxton, Texas's attorney-general, in the state's upcoming Republican primary for a seat in the United States Senate. John Cornyn, the incumbent, "was not supportive of me when times were tough", Mr Trump said. Republicans fear that Mr Paxton—who is being investigated for alleged ethics violations—would lose to James Talarico, a well-funded Democratic state legislator whose Christian faith may make him appealing to moderate voters.

items.headline: Democrats eye Pennsylvania congressional seat
items.blurb: In Pennsylvania's Lehigh Valley, Bob Brooks, a retired firefighter and union leader, won the Democratic primary for a congressional seat. Democrats hope he can help reconnect the party to voters in the working-class district, which Mr Trump won in 2024. In Georgia Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and Biden administration official, comfortably won the Democratic primary for governor. The state has not had a Democratic governor for two decades.

items.headline: IRS barred from auditing Trump family
items.blurb: Todd Blanche, America's acting attorney-general, said that the Internal Revenue Service is "FOREVER BARRED" from continuing any existing audits of the Trump family or its businesses. On Monday the president dropped a lawsuit against the tax agency in which he had demanded $10bn because an IRS contractor had leaked his tax returns. longform.title: Why I don’t buy masculinism
longform.thesis: Masculinism — a movement seeking to reverse feminist gains including women's suffrage and workplace equality — has become the ideological glue of the American right, but its core claim that feminism has ruined America is unsupported and its prescriptions represent a reactionary response to genuine but misdiagnosed male struggles.
longform.context: The piece serves as a promotional author's note for Lewis's June 2026 Atlantic cover story, written against the backdrop of masculinist ideas gaining mainstream political traction, including figures connected to the Trump administration such as Pete Hegseth.
arguments: Masculinism is a coherent ideological movement with named proponents — pastor Douglas Wilson, Raw Egg Nationalist Charles Cornish-Dale, and writer Helen Andrews — who advocate concrete policy reversals including repealing the Nineteenth Amendment, instituting a 'family wage,' and reversing the 'feminization' of professional workplaces.

The movement targets empathy as its symbolic enemy, framing it as 'a dangerous, feminine softness toward immigrants and criminals,' which reveals that masculinism functions less as advocacy for men and more as a vehicle for broader right-wing policy goals on immigration and criminal justice.

Lewis concedes that some male struggles are real and underreported — citing data that the majority of problem gamblers are male — but treats this as distinct from and exploited by masculinist ideology, rejecting the movement's causal claim that feminism is responsible for male decline.

Feminism's success, Lewis argues, is precisely what generates backlash: 'When The Atlantic was founded, in 1857, American women were second-class citizens' — the scale of transformation since then explains the intensity of the reactionary response.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it documents masculinism's move from fringe internet subculture to a force with direct access to federal power, exemplified by Wilson's denominational connection to a sitting Cabinet secretary. Lewis's framing — that misogyny is now 'the single most important force holding together the American right' — positions gender politics as a structural feature of contemporary conservatism, not a peripheral culture-war sideshow. It also raises the stakes for how journalists cover male grievance without laundering reactionary politics.
questions_raised: If some male struggles are genuine and underserved by mainstream discourse, what non-masculinist frameworks exist to address them — and why have those frameworks failed to gain political traction?

Lewis asserts that most women are not 'secretly hankering' for patriarchy's restoration, but the piece does not engage with polling or evidence on this claim, leaving open the question of whether masculinism has broader popular appeal than its critics acknowledge.
